catalog_quote: All the languages dealt with here (W B R S) have, in addition to the types of syllables already described, other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable. Such weak syllables usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur. The tone on such syllables tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch in all four languages. Though this phenomenon would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language, it is so infrequent in the type of words that we are dealing with that we can get along by the simple device of placing a short mark ˘ over the vowel; if we know from slower pronunciation what the reduced tone would have been, we will mark it, for example S măphraaw4 or mă4phraaw4 'coconut.' new_statements.rule_in_words: Tai Dón is a six-tone language whose words are essentially monosyllabic tone-bearing ('normal') syllables. The only stress statement is that a minor class of weakly stressed syllables (short a vowel, tone neutralised to mid level) can be prefixed to a normal syllable, i.e. in the rare sesquisyllabic words the final (main) syllable carries full stress and tone and the presyllable is weak; such words are infrequent in White Tai. No stress rule is stated for monosyllables or for compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the only stress distinction drawn is weak (presyllable) vs normal syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak syllables 'usually' have short a; 'sometimes other vowels occur'; Gedney says the phenomenon 'would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language' and marks such syllables only with a breve.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic word shapes) in citation forms from Gedney's 1964 field notes; a comparative sketch of four languages, not a description of Tai Dón word stress as such. White Tai data = Lai Châu (muang lay) and Muong Te speakers at Tung Nghia.
new_statements.identity_note: Gedney's 'White Tai' = the speech of Lai Châu (muang lay) and Muong Te (muang te) people recorded at the Tung Nghia refugee settlement near Dalat in July 1964 = Tai Dón proper (taid1250). Minot 1940 and Martini 1954 likewise describe the Lai Châu / Muong Te / Phong Thổ variety. Caution on two Glottolog-listed references: Savina 1910 and Bonifacy 1907 describe the Tày of the Clear River, which Gedney (p. 416) explicitly separates from White Tai ('differ greatly in initial consonants'); they belong to Tày (tayy1240 / tyz) rather than taid1250.

sources.note: Front matter written at Muong Te (Lai Châu) 1938. p. 4 'A. Remarques sur la transcription latine' announces 'l'accentuation de ces lettres' and 'l'intonation des mots'; p. 5 'III. Prononciation et accentuation' turns out to be about vowel length only (brèves/longues); p. 6 'IV. Intonations' lists six tones (naturel et égal, ascendant, interrogatif, jeté, élevé, descendant). No statement on word stress. Persée PDF is altcha-gated; page images downloaded via /renderPage/.
